Chromosome Structure
Replicated chromosomes consist of 2 identical halves
Each half: chromatid
Chromatids form as DNA copies itself prior to cell division
As cell divides, each new cell gets 1 chromatid (1 copy of each chromosome) 
Chromatids attach at the centromere
Holds the chromatids together until they separate during division
Important for movement of chromosomes during division
explanation: Replicated chromosomes consist of two identical halves, with each half called a chromatid. Chromatids form when DNA copies itself prior to cell division. When division occurs, each new daughter cell receives one chromatid, ensuring it gets a copy of each chromosome. The two sister chromatids are attached at a specialized region called the centromere, which holds them together until they separate during division and plays an important role in chromosome movement during mitosis/meiosis.

questions.q: What is each identical half of a replicated chromosome called?
questions.exp: Replicated chromosomes consist of 2 identical halves, and each half is called a chromatid.

questions.q: What structure holds two sister chromatids together until they separate during cell division?
questions.exp: Chromatids attach at the centromere, which holds them together until they separate during division.
